touches.text: artifact: the one door a record of truth changes through, and the journal of who came through it (hash-chained, caller read from the kernel). WHY: errors are permanent in records of truth (Law 7), and the journal is what shows a record moved by hand. USERS: everyone who writes a record. [Q#91: The caller class is read from the kernel's cgroup path, so on Windows it reads null and the class comes only from env vars (CAIRN_USER, CLAUDECODE, CAIRN_OPERATOR); gate cannot be reached, and 3 teeth in test_artifact_door.py say UNRAN. Measured 2026-11-12: the Windows parent process chain does show claude.exe above a shell. Is Windows a first-class caller platform (an exe-name chain: claude.exe is cc, a console with no claude above it is akien, a service session is gate), or env-fallback only?]
Shareable provenance (charters, tickets, validations) is git JSON beside the code, never a row.

Commit often. WHY: so we never wind up with stray files or incomplete work. [Q#94: A crossing into PROVEME refuses while anything in either tree is uncommitted (working_tree_clean, widened by ticket c1cca2e3dc23 on your 8w, F11 and 8x; unclaimed dirt refuses too, 8u). So with peers on one box, one peer's ticket records (another ticket's log/state, the artifact journal) block every other peer's crossing. Measured 2026-11-12: 3195b3b834bc's PROVEME was refused twice on the Dell, over d692ef650534's records and then the orchestrator's. Do records that artifact.locate claims for ANOTHER ticket stop blocking (unclaimed dirt and any code dirt still refuse), or does the whole-tree rule stand and peers serialise their crossings per box?]
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).
scratch: a proof's throwaway temp dirs and worktrees, cleaned up by the door. WHY: a run must leave nothing behind (4.3.1.7). USERS: the tester.
Trouble: it has to be able to report when nothing else can, so a direct line makes sense for recovery (6.3.4).
Trouble tickets (3.4.3) live here. Any device has a direct line to raise one, not over the bus (2.3.7.1.3).

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf (Akien, same day: "that could be in the class, rather than the instance :) self queuing"). WHY: Akien, 2026-11-10: "now it has to send it's fileref over to the thing that will process it, and a new code instance created over there even tho it's the same thing... because that's good encapsulation. :)"

Cairn owns all of ~/.cairn/ and delegates each ~/.cairn/devices/ subtree to its device. Everything outside devices/ (~/.cairn/logging/ and the rest) is Cairn's, so every log is Cairn's and Cairn cleans them up in sleep. Transient things are files there; trouble tickets are logging items.
validation_store: reads and writes seals. USERS: the tester.

The certificate is one file type you can't write. It carries a cryptographic (or similar) way to say that the right code wrote it, on this date, at this time, with these hashed findings. That signing belongs in the base gate class, so every gate has it.
